<action type="say">
First, let’s make sure you avoid a burst and water damage. Then we can try to safely thaw it.

1) Immediate safety checks
- Do you see any of this right now: bulging pipe, cracks, dripping, or water on the cabinet floor?
- If YES to any leak: 
  - Immediately close the nearest shutoff valves under the sink (small valve(s) on the supply lines).
  - If you can’t find those, shut off the main water to the house if possible.
  - Put a bucket/towels under the pipe.

2) If it’s frozen but NOT leaking
- Open the faucet (hot and cold) on that sink slightly so it can drip. This relieves pressure as it thaws.
- Leave cabinet doors under the sink open so warm room air can circulate.

3) Safe ways to thaw the pipe
Use ONLY gentle, dry heat, starting from the faucet side and moving back along the pipe:
- Best options:
  - Hair dryer on medium or high, moving it slowly along the exposed pipe.
  - Space heater in the room, pointed near (not directly touching) the area, supervised only.
  - Warm (not boiling) towels wrapped around accessible sections of pipe, replaced as they cool.
- Keep the faucet open while you do this. You should start to hear water trickling as it thaws.

4) What to AVOID
- Do NOT use an open flame (torch, lighter, gas heater) — serious fire risk.
- Do NOT use a heat gun on high very close to the pipe or cabinet — can damage pipes or start a fire.
- Don’t leave space heaters or hair dryers running unattended.

5) Watch for a hidden burst
Even if it’s not leaking yet, a crack might only show when the ice melts:
- Stay nearby while thawing and check frequently for new drips or water sounds in the cabinet, wall, or floor.
- If you suddenly see water spraying or dripping, shut off water immediately (local valve or main).

To tailor this better:
- Is the pipe visible in the cabinet (metal or plastic), or is it mostly inside the wall?
- Do you see any leaks or bulges right now?
- Do you have a hair dryer or small space heater available?

If you tell me your answers (and roughly how cold it is where you are), I can give a more specific step‑by‑step for your exact setup and let you know when it’s time to call a plumber instead of DIY.</action>

<action type="say">
Since the pipe is visible, not leaking, and you have a hair dryer, you’re in a good position to try thawing it.

Do this:

1) Prep and safety
- Find your main water shutoff now (just in case a crack appears when it thaws).
- Clear out the cabinet, lay down towels, and put a bowl or bucket under the pipes.
- Plug the hair dryer into a dry outlet outside the cabinet; keep cord and dryer away from any water.

2) Open faucet and cabinet
- Open both hot and cold on that faucet and leave them open (even if nothing comes out yet).
- Leave the cabinet doors wide open; if you can, turn up the house heat a bit.

3) Thaw with the hair dryer
- Set the dryer to warm/medium or warm/high.
- Start on the pipe section closest to the faucet and the shutoff valves, then work slowly toward where the pipe disappears into the wall/floor.
- Hold the dryer a few inches away, moving it back and forth—don’t blast one spot constantly.
- The pipe should get warm but not so hot you can’t comfortably touch it.

4) Watch for changes
- Listen at the faucet: first sign is usually sputtering or a small trickle, then increasing flow.
- Keep checking under the sink and around where the pipe goes into the wall for any new drips or spraying.
- If you see water leaking/spraying: immediately close the shutoff valves under the sink or, if needed, the main shutoff.

5) Timing / when it might be deeper
- This can take 15–30 minutes of steady, careful warming.
- If after ~30–40 minutes of working along all accessible pipe there is still zero water, the frozen section is likely inside the wall/floor or farther upstream.

To decide the next move, tell me:
- Do other faucets/showers/toilets in the house have normal water flow, or is everything dry?
- Under the sink, do the pipes look like metal (copper/steel) or plastic/PEX (white/gray/blue/red)?

You can start thawing now and let me know if you hear any sputtering, get a trickle, or see any leaks, and I’ll walk you through what to do next based on what happens.</action>

<action type="say">
That bulged section is a serious warning sign — it means the pipe has stretched and is very likely cracked already or will crack as it thaws.

Do this now:

1) Stop active thawing
- Stop using the hair dryer on or near the bulged area immediately. Heating a bulged copper pipe is how it usually turns into a split and a spray.

2) Shut off water feeding that sink
- Under the sink, look for two small shutoff valves on the pipes going up to the faucet (one hot, one cold).
- Turn both valves clockwise all the way until they stop. This isolates just that sink so the rest of the house can still have water.
- If there are no individual shutoffs or they won’t turn, shut off the main water to the house instead.

3) Open the faucet and prep for leaks
- With those valves closed (or main off), leave the kitchen faucet handles open. This relieves pressure as the ice slowly melts.
- Keep towels and a bucket under the bulged section. Watch it periodically — as the ice melts, any existing crack may start dripping.

4) Expect that section to need repair
- A bulged copper pipe is effectively damaged, even if it hasn’t burst open yet. A plumber will usually cut out and replace that section of pipe.
- Until it’s repaired, keep water to that sink OFF. If you see any dripping or spraying at any point, double‑check the shutoff valves are fully closed; if it still leaks, shut the main water and keep catching water with towels/bucket.

If you’d like help lining up a plumber, tell me:
- Your ZIP/postal code or city
- How urgent this is (today vs. sometime in the next few days)

I can then help you estimate cost and find a suitable plumbing service nearby.</action>
